subtopics.title: MySQL Database Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Database Connector for MySQL, including JDBC driver setup, db:my-sql-connection, connection pooling, and select/bulk-insert examples.
subtopics.summary: MySQL integration in Mule 4 uses the generic Database Connector with the MySQL JDBC driver and the db:my-sql-connection element.
subtopics.content_html:
Most enterprise integrations eventually need to read from or write to a relational database, and MySQL is one of the most common targets you'll wire into a Mule application. Rather than shipping a dedicated MySQL connector, MuleSoft handles this through the generic Database Connector, which speaks to MySQL over a standard JDBC driver. Typical use cases include synchronizing order records between a CRM and an e-commerce platform, staging data for a nightly batch load, looking up reference data mid-flow, or writing transformed payloads into a reporting schema.

Adding the MySQL Driver

Because the Database Connector is driver-agnostic, you must add the MySQL JDBC driver as a Maven dependency in your project's pom.xml before the connector can open a connection. Without it, deploying the application throws a ClassNotFoundException at runtime rather than a design-time error.

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
    <version>8.3.0</version>
</dependency>

Global Configuration

The connector exposes a dedicated db:my-sql-connection element that takes host, port, user, password, and database attributes directly, so you don't need to hand-craft a JDBC URL. Connection pooling is configured on the same element through the poolingProfile child, and credentials should always be externalized to a secure properties file rather than hardcoded.

<db:config name="MySQL_Config" doc:name="MySQL Config">
    <db:my-sql-connection host="${db.host}" port="${db.port}"
        user="${db.user}" password="${secure::db.password}"
        database="${db.database}">
        <db:pooling-profile maxPoolSize="10" minPoolSize="2" acquireIncrement="1"/>
    </db:my-sql-connection>
</db:config>

Key Operations

The Database Connector exposes a consistent set of operations regardless of the underlying vendor, which is one of its biggest strengths — you can swap MySQL for PostgreSQL or Oracle later with minimal flow changes.

OperationPurpose
db:selectRuns a parameterized SELECT and returns a streaming or in-memory result set
db:insertInserts a single row and can return generated keys
db:bulk-insertInserts a batch of rows from a collection payload in one round trip
db:update / db:deleteRuns parameterized UPDATE/DELETE statements
db:stored-procedureInvokes a stored procedure, including IN/OUT parameters

Example Flow

The flow below queries orders for a given status and then bulk-inserts an archive copy of any rows returned, all using bound parameters to avoid SQL injection.

<flow name="archive-shipped-orders">
    <db:select config-ref="MySQL_Config">
        <db:sql>SELECT id, customer_id, total, status FROM orders WHERE status = :status</db:sql>
        <db:input-parameters>#[{status: 'SHIPPED'}]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:select>

    <db:bulk-insert config-ref="MySQL_Config">
        <db:sql>INSERT INTO orders_archive (id, customer_id, total, status) VALUES (:id, :customer_id, :total, :status)</db:sql>
        <db:input-parameters>#[payload]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:bulk-insert>
</flow>
Tip: Always bind values with named parameters (:paramName) instead of concatenating DataWeave expressions into the SQL string. Concatenation defeats prepared-statement caching and opens the door to SQL injection.

Transactions

When a flow performs multiple write operations that must succeed or fail together, wrap them in a <try> scope with a transactional action, or set the transaction type at the operation level. The Database Connector participates in Mule's local transaction manager, so a rollback on error will undo every statement executed within the transactional boundary.

  • MySQL access goes through the generic Database Connector plus the MySQL JDBC driver, not a dedicated MySQL-only connector.
  • Use db:my-sql-connection for readable, vendor-specific connection attributes instead of a raw JDBC URL.
  • Always parameterize SQL with named bindings and store credentials in a secure properties file.
  • Use db:bulk-insert for batch writes and wrap multi-statement writes in a transaction when atomicity matters.

subtopics.title: FTP Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how to configure the Mule 4 FTP Connector for polling remote directories, reading and writing files, and archiving processed files with ftp:listener.
subtopics.summary: The FTP Connector polls remote directories and reads or writes files using ftp:config, ftp:listener, ftp:read, and ftp:write.
subtopics.content_html:
File-based integration hasn't gone away, and plenty of trading partners, mainframes, and legacy systems still exchange data exclusively through FTP. The FTP Connector lets a Mule application poll a remote directory for new files, write output files, and manage file lifecycle operations like listing, renaming, and deleting — all without writing custom socket code.

Typical Use Cases

You'll reach for the FTP Connector when a partner drops nightly CSV extracts into a shared directory that Mule needs to pick up and transform, when a downstream mainframe batch job expects fixed-width files delivered on a schedule, or when an internal system publishes flat files that other applications consume asynchronously.

Global Configuration

The ftp:config element wraps an ftp:connection that carries the host, port, credentials, and working directory. Because plain FTP transmits credentials and data unencrypted, it should be reserved for internal networks or legacy systems that genuinely have no SFTP/FTPS option.

<ftp:config name="FTP_Config" doc:name="FTP Config">
    <ftp:connection host="${ftp.host}" port="${ftp.port}"
        username="${ftp.username}" password="${secure::ftp.password}"
        workingDir="/outbound" connectionTimeout="30" connectionTimeoutUnit="SECONDS"/>
</ftp:config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
ftp:listenerMessage source that polls a directory and triggers a flow for each matching file
ftp:readReads a specific file into the payload as a stream
ftp:writeWrites the current payload to a remote file, with append or overwrite modes
ftp:listLists files in a directory, optionally filtered and recursive
ftp:copy / ftp:rename / ftp:deleteManages file lifecycle after processing

Example Flow

This flow polls an inbound directory every 60 seconds, converts each CSV to JSON, writes the result to an outbound directory, and then moves the source file into a processed folder so it isn't picked up twice.

<flow name="ftp-inbound-csv-flow">
    <ftp:listener config-ref="FTP_Config" directory="/inbound" autoDelete="false">
        <scheduling-strategy>
            <fixed-frequency frequency="60000"/>
        </scheduling-strategy>
        <ftp:matcher filenamePattern="*.csv"/>
    </ftp:listener>

    <ee:transform doc:name="CSV to JSON">
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>

    <ftp:write config-ref="FTP_Config" path="/outbound/#[attributes.fileName replace '.csv' with '.json']"/>

    <ftp:copy config-ref="FTP_Config" path="#[attributes.path]" targetPath="/processed" doc:name="Archive source file"/>
    <ftp:delete config-ref="FTP_Config" path="#[attributes.path]"/>
</flow>
Note: The ftp:listener attribute autoDelete removes the source file immediately after it's read into the flow. Set it to false when you need the original file available later in the flow for archiving, as shown above.

Error Handling and Reliability

Network blips are common with FTP, so configure reconnection strategies on the connection and consider a watermark or idempotent message filter if the same file could be reprocessed after a partial failure. For high-volume directories, prefer ftp:listener over manual polling with ftp:list, since the listener already tracks which files have been processed.

Choosing Between FTP and Its Secure Alternatives

Before settling on plain FTP, confirm the partner genuinely cannot support FTPS (FTP over TLS) or SFTP. Many "legacy" FTP requirements turn out to be a default configuration rather than a hard constraint, and moving to an encrypted transport removes an entire class of credential-exposure risk with only a small configuration change on the Mule side. Where FTP is unavoidable, isolate the traffic on a private network segment or VPN tunnel rather than exposing it over the open internet.

Note: The FTP Connector and the SFTP Connector share a very similar operation set — read, write, list, listener — which makes migrating a flow from FTP to SFTP largely a matter of swapping the config element and connection attributes rather than rewriting flow logic.
  • FTP is unencrypted; use it only for trusted internal networks or when a partner has no SFTP/FTPS alternative.
  • The ftp:listener source handles polling and file-matching so you don't have to build your own scheduler around ftp:list.
  • Always plan a post-processing strategy — move, rename, or delete — so files aren't reprocessed on the next poll.
  • Evaluate FTPS or SFTP first; the operation set is similar enough that migrating later is straightforward.

subtopics.title: SFTP Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 SFTP Connector with password or SSH key-based authentication, sftp:listener watermarking, and full read/write flow examples in XML.
subtopics.summary: The SFTP Connector securely transfers files over SSH using sftp:config with password or identity-file authentication and the listener, read, and write operations.
subtopics.content_html:
SFTP is the connector you'll actually use in production far more often than plain FTP, since it layers file transfer on top of the SSH protocol and encrypts both the authentication handshake and the data in transit. Anywhere a business partner requires a secure file drop — EDI documents, payment batches, healthcare claims — SFTP is the de facto standard, and Mule's SFTP Connector supports both password and public-key authentication out of the box.

Global Configuration

An sftp:config wraps an sftp:connection. Port 22 is the SSH default, and you can authenticate either with a username/password pair or, more securely, with a private key file referenced through identityFile and an optional passphrase.

<sftp:config name="SFTP_Config" doc:name="SFTP Config">
    <sftp:connection host="${sftp.host}" port="22"
        username="${sftp.username}"
        identityFile="${sftp.keyPath}"
        passphrase="${secure::sftp.keyPassphrase}"
        connectionTimeout="30" connectionTimeoutUnit="SECONDS">
        <reconnection>
            <reconnect frequency="5000" count="3"/>
        </reconnection>
    </sftp:connection>
</sftp:config>

For simple password authentication, swap identityFile/passphrase for a password attribute pointing at a secure property. Most partner integrations, however, will supply you with a private key and ask for your public key to be added to their authorized_keys file.

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
sftp:listenerMessage source that watches a directory and fires per new/modified file
sftp:readStreams a remote file's contents into the payload
sftp:writeWrites the payload to a remote path, supporting OVERWRITE, APPEND, and fail if exists modes
sftp:listLists directory contents with optional recursion and matcher filters
sftp:delete / sftp:renameCleans up or archives files after processing

Example Flow

The flow below listens for new invoice files, validates the payload against a schema, and writes the confirmed file to an outbound directory for a downstream ERP pickup.

<flow name="sftp-invoice-inbound-flow">
    <sftp:listener config-ref="SFTP_Config" directory="/partner/inbound" watermarkEnabled="true">
        <scheduling-strategy>
            <fixed-frequency frequency="30000"/>
        </scheduling-strategy>
        <sftp:matcher filenamePattern="invoice-*.xml"/>
    </sftp:listener>

    <validation:is-true expression="#[payload startsWith '<Invoice'"]" doc:name="Basic shape check"/>

    <sftp:write config-ref="SFTP_Config"
        path="/erp/outbound/#[attributes.fileName]"
        mode="OVERWRITE"/>
</flow>
Tip: Enable watermarkEnabled="true" on sftp:listener so Mule only processes files newer than the last recorded timestamp. This prevents reprocessing the entire directory after an application restart.

Security Considerations

Prefer key-based authentication over passwords whenever the partner supports it, and rotate keys according to your organization's security policy. Store the private key and any passphrase outside of source control — typically in a secrets manager or an encrypted properties file — and restrict the SFTP user's home directory with chroot on the server side if you control it.

Working with High-Volume or Large-File Transfers

The sftp:read and sftp:write operations stream by default, so large files — multi-gigabyte exports, for instance — don't need to fit entirely in heap memory. When a directory listener has to process thousands of files per cycle, tune maxConcurrency on the containing flow to control how many transfers run in parallel, since opening too many simultaneous SSH sessions against the same remote server can trigger rate limiting or connection refusals on the partner's side.

Tip: If a remote server enforces strict host key checking, configure a known-hosts file on the connection rather than disabling host key verification; skipping verification defeats much of the security benefit SFTP provides in the first place.
  • SFTP encrypts both credentials and payload over SSH, making it the preferred choice over plain FTP for partner integrations.
  • Use identityFile and passphrase for key-based authentication instead of passwords when possible.
  • Turn on watermarking in sftp:listener to avoid reprocessing files after a redeploy or restart.
  • Stream large files by default and tune maxConcurrency to avoid overwhelming the remote server.

subtopics.title: Amazon S3 Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Amazon S3 Connector with access-key or IAM role authentication, then use the create-object, get-object, and list-objects operations.
subtopics.summary: The Amazon S3 Connector reads, writes, lists, and deletes objects in S3 buckets using s3:config with static credentials or an IAM instance role.
subtopics.content_html:
Cloud object storage has become a default landing zone for everything from data lake ingestion to document archival, and Amazon S3 is the most widely used implementation. The Amazon S3 Connector lets a Mule flow create, retrieve, list, copy, and delete objects in a bucket, making it a natural fit for staging files before a batch job, archiving processed documents, or serving as the backing store for a document management API.

Typical Use Cases

Common patterns include landing inbound files from a partner into a raw bucket before transformation, writing generated PDFs or reports for later retrieval, archiving processed SFTP files for compliance retention, and building a lightweight file API on top of S3 pre-signed URLs.

Global Configuration

The s3:config element wraps a connection that authenticates either with a static access key/secret key pair or, in EC2/ECS deployments, with an IAM instance role and no static credentials at all. When static credentials are used, they should always be pulled from a secure properties file rather than embedded in the flow.

<s3:config name="S3_Config" doc:name="S3 Config">
    <s3:connection accessKey="${s3.accessKey}" secretKey="${secure::s3.secretKey}"
        region="US_EAST_1"/>
</s3:config>
Tip: When running on AWS compute with an attached IAM role, omit accessKey/secretKey entirely and let the connector fall back to the default AWS credentials provider chain. This avoids storing long-lived secrets altogether.

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
s3:create-objectUploads a payload as a new object under a given key
s3:get-objectRetrieves an object's content as a stream
s3:list-objectsLists object keys in a bucket, optionally filtered by prefix
s3:copy-objectCopies an object within or across buckets
s3:delete-objectRemoves an object by key
s3:create-presigned-uriGenerates a temporary, signed download/upload URL

Example Flow

This flow lists objects under a prefix representing today's inbound batch, then downloads and republishes each one for downstream processing.

<flow name="s3-process-daily-batch">
    <s3:list-objects config-ref="S3_Config" bucketName="acme-inbound"
        prefix="batch/#[now() as String {format: 'yyyy-MM-dd'}]/"/>

    <foreach>
        <s3:get-object config-ref="S3_Config" bucketName="acme-inbound"
            key="#[payload.key]" target="fileContent"/>

        <s3:create-object config-ref="S3_Config" bucketName="acme-processed"
            key="processed/#[payload.key]"
            body="#[vars.fileContent]"/>
    </foreach>
</flow>

Performance and Cost Notes

For large objects, favor streaming (the default for s3:get-object) over loading the full payload into memory, and set an explicit storageClass on s3:create-object when writing archival data to control cost. Batch listing operations with pagination (maxKeys) when a bucket may contain more objects than fit comfortably in one response.

Securing Access to a Bucket

Scope the IAM policy attached to your access key or instance role as tightly as possible — grant only the actions the flow actually needs, such as s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on a specific bucket prefix, rather than broad account-wide S3 permissions. When external parties need temporary access to a single object, generate a time-limited link with s3:create-presigned-uri instead of sharing bucket credentials, and keep the expiration window as short as the use case allows.

Tip: Enable server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) on buckets holding sensitive data, and configure the connector's create-object operation to set the appropriate encryption headers rather than relying solely on bucket-level defaults.
  • Prefer IAM instance roles over static access keys when the Mule app runs on AWS infrastructure.
  • Use s3:list-objects with a prefix filter to scope operations instead of scanning an entire bucket.
  • Stream large objects rather than buffering them fully in memory during get-object/create-object.
  • Scope IAM permissions narrowly and prefer presigned URLs over shared credentials for temporary external access.

subtopics.title: Azure Service Bus Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Azure Service Bus Connector for queues and topics, including publish, listener, and peek-lock complete and abandon message examples.
subtopics.summary: The Azure Service Bus Connector publishes and consumes messages from Azure queues and topics using a connection string and peek-lock message handling.
subtopics.content_html:
Organizations standardized on Microsoft Azure frequently use Azure Service Bus as their enterprise messaging backbone, and the Azure Service Bus Connector lets Mule applications publish and consume messages from that same infrastructure without introducing a second broker. It supports both the simple queue point-to-point pattern and the publish/subscribe pattern through topics and subscriptions, which makes it suitable for anything from order processing pipelines to fan-out event notification.

Queues vs. Topics and Subscriptions

A queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer, which suits classic request-processing workloads such as a single order-fulfillment service reading orders one at a time. A topic, by contrast, broadcasts each message to every subscription registered on it, so multiple independent consumers — say, billing, shipping, and analytics — can each process the same event without competing for it.

Global Configuration

The connector authenticates using either a full connection string (containing a Shared Access Signature key) copied from the Azure portal, or individual SAS policy name/key pairs. The connection string approach is the most common because Azure generates it for you directly against the namespace or entity.

<azure-service-bus:config name="ServiceBus_Config" doc:name="Azure Service Bus Config">
    <azure-service-bus:connection connectionString="${secure::asb.connectionString}"/>
</azure-service-bus:config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
azure-service-bus:publishSends a message to a queue or topic
azure-service-bus:on-new-message-listenerMessage source that consumes from a queue or a topic subscription
azure-service-bus:complete-messageAcknowledges a message so it is removed from the entity (peek-lock mode)
azure-service-bus:abandon-messageReleases the lock and returns the message to the entity for redelivery
azure-service-bus:dead-letter-messageMoves a poison message to the dead-letter sub-queue

Example Flow

This flow publishes an order-created event to a topic, and a second flow consumes it from a dedicated subscription, completing the message only after successful processing.

<flow name="publish-order-event">
    <azure-service-bus:publish config-ref="ServiceBus_Config"
        destination="orders-topic" destinationType="TOPIC">
        <azure-service-bus:body>#[write(payload, 'application/json')]</azure-service-bus:body>
    </azure-service-bus:publish>
</flow>

<flow name="consume-billing-subscription">
    <azure-service-bus:on-new-message-listener config-ref="ServiceBus_Config"
        destination="orders-topic" subscriptionName="billing-subscription"
        receiveAndDeleteModeEnabled="false"/>

    <try>
        <flow-ref name="process-billing-event"/>
        <azure-service-bus:complete-message lockToken="#[attributes.lockToken]"/>
    <error-handler>
        <on-error-continue>
            <azure-service-bus:abandon-message lockToken="#[attributes.lockToken]"/>
        </on-error-continue>
    </error-handler>
    </try>
</flow>
Note: Leaving receiveAndDeleteModeEnabled false puts the entity in peek-lock mode, meaning a message stays invisible but not removed until you explicitly complete, abandon, or dead-letter it. This gives you at-least-once delivery semantics with room to retry.

Sizing and Tier Considerations

Azure Service Bus is offered in Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers, and the tier you provision directly affects which features are available to your Mule flows. Topics and sessions, for instance, require at least the Standard tier, so confirm the namespace tier matches the entity types your integration design assumes before you build against it. Premium namespaces add dedicated throughput and larger message sizes, which matters for high-volume event pipelines moving large payloads.

When a consuming flow needs strict message ordering within a logical group — for example, all events for a single order — enable sessions on the queue or subscription and set a sessionId on publish so Service Bus routes related messages to the same consumer in order.

  • Choose queues for point-to-point workloads and topics/subscriptions when multiple independent consumers need the same event.
  • Peek-lock mode plus explicit completion is the safest default for reliable processing; avoid receive-and-delete unless duplicate loss is acceptable.
  • Store the Service Bus connection string as a secure property, never inline in the flow XML.
  • Confirm your namespace tier supports the entity types (topics, sessions) your flow design depends on.

subtopics.title: ActiveMQ Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Connect Mule 4 to ActiveMQ using the generic JMS Connector's jms:active-mq-connection, covering broker URLs, listener, publish, and acknowledgment modes.
subtopics.summary: ActiveMQ integration in Mule 4 uses the generic JMS Connector configured with jms:active-mq-connection and an OpenWire broker URL.
subtopics.content_html:
Unlike some of the other messaging systems in this catalog, ActiveMQ doesn't have a connector bearing its own name in Anypoint Exchange. Instead, Mule talks to ActiveMQ through the generic JMS Connector, which speaks the JMS 1.1/2.0 API that ActiveMQ implements. This makes ActiveMQ a natural fit for organizations already running it as an on-premises broker for order queues, event notifications, or decoupling legacy Java EE applications from newer services.

Adding the ActiveMQ Client Library

The JMS Connector needs a JMS provider implementation on the classpath to actually talk to ActiveMQ; add the ActiveMQ client as a Maven dependency alongside the connector.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.activemq</groupId>
    <artifactId>activemq-client</artifactId>
    <version>5.18.3</version>
</dependency>

Global Configuration

The jms:config element takes a jms:active-mq-connection that wires up an ActiveMQ connection factory pointed at a broker URL, typically using the OpenWire protocol on port 61616. You can supply a factory bean directly or reference one built from the connection URL and credentials.

<jms:config name="JMS_Config" doc:name="JMS Config">
    <jms:active-mq-connection username="${amq.username}" password="${secure::amq.password}">
        <jms:factory-configuration brokerUrl="tcp://${amq.host}:61616"/>
    </jms:active-mq-connection>
    <jms:caching-strategy>
        <jms:default-caching/>
    </jms:caching-strategy>
</jms:config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
jms:listenerMessage source that subscribes to a queue or topic destination
jms:publishSends a message to a queue or topic
jms:consumePulls a single message synchronously (request-style consumption)
jms:ackManually acknowledges a message when using CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE mode

Example Flow

This flow listens on a queue for incoming order messages, processes them, and publishes a confirmation onto a downstream topic for interested subscribers.

<flow name="amq-order-processing-flow">
    <jms:listener config-ref="JMS_Config" destination="orders.queue" ackMode="AUTO"/>

    <ee:transform doc:name="Enrich order">
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload ++ {processedAt: now()}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>

    <jms:publish config-ref="JMS_Config" destination="orders.confirmed.topic" destinationType="TOPIC"/>
</flow>
Tip: Set ackMode="AUTO" for simple fire-and-forget processing, but switch to MANUAL with an explicit jms:ack call when you need to guarantee a message is only removed from the queue after downstream side effects — like a database write — have succeeded.

Durability and Redelivery

For topics, configure a durable subscriber name if consumers may be offline when a message is published; otherwise messages published while no subscriber is connected are lost. ActiveMQ also supports dead-letter queues for messages that exceed their redelivery count, which is worth pairing with Mule's error handling so poison messages don't loop indefinitely.

Connecting to a Clustered or Failover Broker

Production ActiveMQ deployments are rarely a single node. When the broker runs in a master/slave or network-of-brokers topology, use a failover transport URL instead of a single tcp:// address so the client automatically reconnects to a surviving broker if the primary goes down.

<jms:factory-configuration brokerUrl="failover:(tcp://broker1:61616,tcp://broker2:61616)?randomize=false"/>

This URL syntax tells the ActiveMQ client library to try each broker in order and keep retrying transparently, which is far more resilient than hardcoding a single host and relying on Mule's own reconnection strategy alone.

  • ActiveMQ is accessed through the generic JMS Connector, using jms:active-mq-connection and an OpenWire broker URL, not a dedicated ActiveMQ connector.
  • Choose manual acknowledgment when message loss on downstream failure is unacceptable.
  • Use durable subscriptions on topics so offline consumers don't silently miss messages.
  • Use a failover broker URL in production so the client survives a broker failover without manual intervention.

subtopics.title: Anypoint MQ Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Anypoint MQ Connector with Connected App credentials, covering queues vs exchanges, FIFO queues, publish, and subscriber operations.
subtopics.summary: Anypoint MQ is MuleSoft's managed cloud messaging service, configured with anypoint-mq:config and used through publish, subscriber, ack, and nack operations.
subtopics.content_html:
Anypoint MQ is MuleSoft's own cloud-native messaging service, fully managed within the Anypoint Platform, and it's frequently the default choice when a project is already standardized on CloudHub and doesn't want to stand up and operate a separate broker. Because it's provisioned through Anypoint Platform itself, queues and exchanges are managed the same way as APIs and applications — with environment separation, role-based access, and built-in monitoring in Anypoint Monitoring.

Queues, Exchanges, and FIFO

An Anypoint MQ queue behaves like a standard point-to-point destination. An exchange, paired with one or more bound queues, gives you publish/subscribe fan-out similar to a topic in other brokers. Every queue can be provisioned as either Standard, which prioritizes throughput and allows occasional out-of-order or duplicate delivery, or FIFO, which guarantees strict ordering and exactly-once processing within a message group at the cost of some throughput.

Global Configuration

The anypoint-mq:config element authenticates with a Connected App's client ID and client secret (or legacy queue-level credentials), and it targets a specific Anypoint MQ region and environment tied to your organization.

<anypoint-mq:config name="AnypointMQ_Config" doc:name="Anypoint MQ Config">
    <anypoint-mq:connection clientId="${amq.clientId}" clientSecret="${secure::amq.clientSecret}"
        url="https://mq-us-east-1.anypoint.mulesoft.com/api/v1"/>
</anypoint-mq:config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
anypoint-mq:publishPublishes a message to a queue or exchange
anypoint-mq:subscriberMessage source that continuously receives messages from a queue
anypoint-mq:consumePulls a single message on demand rather than continuously
anypoint-mq:ack / anypoint-mq:nackConfirms successful processing or requeues a failed message

Example Flow

This flow publishes a payment event to an exchange for fan-out, and a companion flow subscribes to a bound queue, acknowledging each message only after it's processed successfully.

<flow name="publish-payment-event">
    <anypoint-mq:publish config-ref="AnypointMQ_Config" destination="payments-exchange">
        <anypoint-mq:body>#[write(payload, 'application/json')]</anypoint-mq:body>
    </anypoint-mq:publish>
</flow>

<flow name="consume-payments-queue" maxConcurrency="4">
    <anypoint-mq:subscriber config-ref="AnypointMQ_Config" destination="payments-notifications-queue"
        acknowledgementMode="MANUAL"/>

    <try>
        <flow-ref name="record-payment-notification"/>
        <anypoint-mq:ack messageAckId="#[attributes.ackId]"/>
    <error-handler>
        <on-error-continue>
            <anypoint-mq:nack messageAckId="#[attributes.ackId]"/>
        </on-error-continue>
    </error-handler>
    </try>
</flow>
Tip: Set maxConcurrency on the flow containing an anypoint-mq:subscriber to control how many messages are processed in parallel, and pair manual acknowledgment with a dead-letter queue so repeatedly failing messages don't block the queue indefinitely.

When to Choose Anypoint MQ

Anypoint MQ removes the operational burden of running and patching a broker, integrates natively with CloudHub networking and security, and is billed per message rather than per server, which suits bursty workloads. Teams with an existing enterprise messaging standard — ActiveMQ, Azure Service Bus, Kafka — often keep that broker for cross-platform needs and use Anypoint MQ specifically for Mule-to-Mule communication.

Dead-Letter Queues and Monitoring

Every Anypoint MQ queue can be configured with a dead-letter queue that automatically receives messages after they exceed a maximum delivery count, preventing a single malformed message from blocking an otherwise healthy queue. Anypoint Monitoring surfaces queue depth, message age, and throughput out of the box, which makes it straightforward to set an alert when a queue's backlog grows past an expected threshold — often a sign that a downstream consumer has stalled or is failing to acknowledge messages.

Client applications authenticate through a Connected App rather than embedding a static API key, which lets an administrator revoke or rotate access centrally without redeploying every Mule application that publishes or subscribes to a given queue.

  • Choose FIFO queues when strict ordering and exactly-once delivery matter more than raw throughput.
  • Use exchanges when multiple independent queues need a copy of the same published message.
  • Manual acknowledgment combined with a dead-letter queue is the safest pattern for production consumers.
  • Monitor queue depth and message age in Anypoint Monitoring to catch stalled consumers early.

subtopics.title: Email Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Email Connector's SMTP, IMAP, and POP3 elements to send mail, poll inboxes for new messages, and process email attachments correctly.
subtopics.summary: The Email Connector sends mail through email:smtp-config and receives it through email:imap-config or email:pop3-config, including attachment handling.
subtopics.content_html:
Email remains a surprisingly common integration surface — sending transactional notifications, routing inbound support requests into a case management system, or processing invoices that partners still send as attachments. The Email Connector covers both directions: an SMTP configuration for sending mail and IMAP or POP3 configurations for retrieving it, each modeled as separate global elements since sending and receiving use fundamentally different protocols.

Sending Email with SMTP

The email:smtp-config element defines the outbound mail server connection, including host, port, credentials, and whether to use STARTTLS. Most modern providers require authentication and encryption, so a typical configuration enables TLS on port 587.

<email:smtp-config name="SMTP_Config" doc:name="SMTP Config">
    <email:smtp-connection host="${smtp.host}" port="587"
        user="${smtp.user}" password="${secure::smtp.password}">
        <email:client-tls-context>
            <tls:trust-store insecure="false"/>
        </email:client-tls-context>
    </email:smtp-connection>
</email:smtp-config>

Receiving Email with IMAP or POP3

Use email:imap-config when you need to browse folders, search, and leave messages on the server after reading — the more capable and commonly used protocol. Use email:pop3-config for simpler mailboxes where messages are downloaded and typically removed from the server.

<email:imap-config name="IMAP_Config" doc:name="IMAP Config">
    <email:imap-connection host="${imap.host}" port="993"
        user="${imap.user}" password="${secure::imap.password}">
        <email:client-tls-context>
            <tls:trust-store insecure="false"/>
        </email:client-tls-context>
    </email:imap-connection>
</email:imap-config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
email:sendSends an email, optionally with attachments and HTML body
email:list-imap / email:list-pop3Retrieves messages from a mailbox, with filtering by criteria such as unread or subject
email:on-new-email-listenerMessage source that triggers a flow when new mail arrives
email:mark-as-read / email:deleteManages message state after processing to avoid reprocessing

Example Flow

This flow polls an inbox for unread messages with attachments, extracts each attachment for downstream processing, and sends a confirmation email once complete.

<flow name="process-invoice-inbox">
    <email:on-new-email-listener config-ref="IMAP_Config" mailboxFolder="INBOX">
        <scheduling-strategy>
            <fixed-frequency frequency="60000"/>
        </scheduling-strategy>
        <email:matcher subjectRegex="Invoice.*" hasAttachments="true"/>
    </email:on-new-email-listener>

    <foreach collection="#[payload.attachments]">
        <flow-ref name="store-invoice-attachment"/>
    </foreach>

    <email:send config-ref="SMTP_Config" subject="Invoice received" toAddresses="#[[attributes.from[0].address]]">
        <email:body contentType="text/plain"><![CDATA[Thanks, your invoice has been received and is being processed.]]></email:body>
    </email:send>

    <email:mark-as-read config-ref="IMAP_Config" emailId="#[attributes.id]"/>
</flow>
Note: Attachments arrive as a collection of parts on the payload, each with its own content type and stream; iterate over payload.attachments rather than assuming a single attachment per message.

Practical Considerations

Always mark messages as read or move them to a processed folder after handling them, otherwise a polling listener will pick up the same email on every cycle. For outbound mail at scale, consider a dedicated transactional email provider's API instead of raw SMTP, since many providers throttle or flag high-volume SMTP traffic from unfamiliar IP ranges.

Sending Attachments and HTML Content

The email:send operation accepts multiple email:attachment elements alongside the body, and each attachment can reference a file on disk, a stream from a previous operation, or bytes computed in DataWeave. Set the body's contentType to text/html when you need rich formatting, and remember that most mail clients still render plain text as a fallback, so pairing an HTML body with meaningful subject lines improves deliverability and readability across clients.

Tip: Test outbound email against a disposable inbox service or an SMTP sandbox (such as a provider's sandbox mode) during development, so test runs never accidentally deliver to real customer addresses.
  • Sending and receiving mail use separate global configs: email:smtp-config for outbound, email:imap-config/email:pop3-config for inbound.
  • IMAP supports folder browsing and leaving mail on the server; POP3 is simpler and typically download-and-remove.
  • Always mark-as-read or delete processed messages to prevent a polling listener from reprocessing the same inbox.
  • Use an SMTP sandbox during development so test flows never send real email to customers.
